bc_stave_dam_trail.blurb:
A small cluster of mossy bluffs and boulders tucked into the forest above Stave Lake near Mission, in the Fraser Valley. Most of the climbing is bouldering, mainly in the VB to V4 range, with a handful of top-rope lines on the little cliffs. The problems sit right beside the hiking trail, so there is almost no walking.

The thick tree canopy keeps the rocks shaded for most of the day, which suits warm weather but means the moss and ferns hold moisture. Give the rock a good while to dry after rain before trying anything.
bc_stave_dam_trail.parking_note: Past the dam on Dewdney Trunk Road, drive up the steep road through a few switchbacks. A gravel lot sits on the left once you clear the last bend.
bc_stave_dam_trail.approach: A short stroll on the trail up the switchbacks from the lot; the rocks are just beside the path.

ca_afpa_rock.blurb:
A modest, friendly formation in the Quail Springs section of Joshua Tree, sitting just over the road from the picnic area lot. Most of the climbing is traditional crack and face climbing on knobby desert rock, with a scattering of top-rope lines and boulder problems around the base. Grades cluster in the moderate range, mainly 5.7 to 5.10, which makes it a good stop for a relaxed day.

The most-used side faces the road, and the walk-in takes only a couple of minutes. The top is breezy, while the base can be sheltered. Descend by walking off the back of the formation.
ca_afpa_rock.parking_note: Use the paved lot at the Quail Springs picnic area, or pull fully off the pavement along the road in front of the rock.
ca_afpa_rock.approach: A couple hundred yards across the road from the picnic area.

ca_gardens_the.blurb:
A bouldering zone among the small cliffs and boulders on the southern slope of Gold Mountain, above Big Bear City. The problems here are mostly short and approachable: the bulk fall at VB to V1, with a few harder lines up in the V4 to V6 range. That makes it a good place for beginners or a mellow warm-up session.

The hillside faces south, so it gets plenty of sun and stays comfortable on cold days. Trails crisscross the slope and the walk up is steep, so expect to climb a bit to reach the rocks. Easter Island is one of the favored easy problems.

ca_stately_pleasure_dome.blurb:
A big granite dome rising above Tenaya Lake, right beside Tioga Road in the Tuolumne high country. Its slabs hold long, mostly moderate friction and crack routes, with many multi-pitch lines from 5.6 up through the 5.11s. Classics include Great White Book, South Crack, Black Angel and Arch Rival, plus Far West Country at an easier grade.

The roadside setting means quick access and plenty of tourists watching. Bolts can be sparse and the climbing runout in places, so be ready for sustained slab moves. The walk-off descent heads west over low-angle slabs; some parties prefer to rappel with two ropes.

ca_gong_show_wall.blurb:
The main attraction of Rock Creek, a high-elevation Sierra canyon above Bishop and Mammoth. The granite here carries a nice mix of sport and trad, with plenty in the 5.10 and 5.11 range and a good run of 5.12s and one 5.13 for stronger climbers. Sideshow, He She, Gong Show, Last Exit and Anything Goes are among the favorites.

The canyon sits around 7,500 feet, so it is mostly a summer and early fall destination. Reaching the base means crossing a stream on logs and then following a well-built path up a talus slope.
ca_gong_show_wall.approach: Cross the creek on fallen logs, then climb a built trail up the talus slope to the base.

ca_mayhem_cove.blurb:
A steep sport crag above the west shore of Lake Tahoe, tucked into Eagle Creek Canyon with views toward Emerald Bay. The granite is vertical to overhanging and heavily featured, so most routes suit climbers comfortable at 5.11 and up, with the bulk in the 5.11 to 5.12 range and a handful of 5.13s. Cajun Hell, Huntin' Gator and Psycho II are the standouts, while Delivering the Goods is a gentler 5.10a.

The left side shades up around midday and the right side a little later, so you can chase sun or shade as the season demands. Most routes have lowering hardware.
ca_mayhem_cove.approach: A short, steep scramble through pines and talus uphill from the trailhead lot.

ca_main_slab_lower.blurb:
The lower half of the Main Slab at Big Rock, a long-loved granite crag above Lake Perris. Climbing is mostly trad on crack and face routes from 5.6 through 5.11, with a few bolted lines and top-ropes. Dark Angel (aka The Ghost), The Shroud and Edger Sanction are among the better lines, and Welcome to Big Rock gives an easy sport option.

The approach is on open, exposed ground with little shade, so summer afternoons can feel baked. Cooler months and early starts are friendlier. Anchors on the slab have been replaced with stainless hardware.

ca_discovery_wall.blurb:
One of the nearest cliffs to the East Side entrance of Pinnacles, set among the volcanic spires. Expect a mix of trad and sport on breccia, with a large share of routes at 5.11 and a decent number around 5.10. Ordeal is the easy classic at 5.8, while The Verdict (direct), Cosmos and Broken Arrow are popular harder sport lines, and Forty Days of Rain is a demanding trad test.

The rock is weaker than granite, so tap holds, treat old bolts with suspicion, and watch for poison oak on the approach. Temperatures can swing a lot over a day.
ca_discovery_wall.parking_note: Leave the car at the Bear Gulch day-use zone on the park's east side and follow the marked access trails.
ca_discovery_wall.approach: Roughly a quarter hour on marked trails from the Bear Gulch day-use area.

ca_bear_the.blurb:
The hardest and steepest of the sport cliffs on Mount St. Helena, a big overhanging volcanic face about a hundred yards wide. Grades climb steadily from left to right, from 5.7s up to a couple of 5.13s, with the bulk at 5.10 to 5.12. Beast of Burden, Treasure Island and Kill Uncle are standouts, with Rampage a more modest 5.10c.

The wall faces east to southeast and sees sun for much of the morning, with the right side shading first. Rock gets looser toward the right, and loose debris above second-pitch lines means belayers should wear helmets.
ca_bear_the.approach: Head up the fire road past the cliff, then take the narrow trail that doubles back through manzanita; allow 20 to 45 minutes from the road.
